about: Feedback written to Ember on her work. Public: codename only, never a real name, school or teacher. Parent notes and level estimates stay private.

entries.subject: Science
entries.title: Moments from scratch
entries.summary: A strong session. You got M = F × d, the see-saw and the metre-rule balance right first time, and your last notebook answer was a proper linked explanation: “the distance is longer and a smaller force is needed”. Three things to fix, all small.
entries.next: Do Science Week 4: moments and the lever chain. It is built around these three fixes. Then say the long-spanner chain out loud without looking.

items.q: Lorry ramp: why is it easier to pull the rope?
items.good: “The rope is further from the hinge… the distance is longer from the pivot” got the first mark. Your self-mark of 1 / 2 was exactly right.
items.fix: You finished with “the moment is larger”. The ramp needs the same moment to lower it either way, so the point is that the force can be smaller. AQA only gives the second mark for “so a smaller force is needed”.
items.model: The rope is further from the hinge, so the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the force is greater. The ramp needs the same moment to lower it, so a smaller force is needed on the rope.

items.good: In Room 4 you said a child on the left turns the see-saw anticlockwise. That is right.
items.fix: Room 4, question 1 and your Room 5 notebook had it backwards (“weights on the left side turns clockwise”). Picture a clock: pushing down on the right makes the right end go from 3 towards 6, which is clockwise.
items.model: A weight on the right of the pivot turns the rule clockwise. A weight on the left turns it anticlockwise. It balances when the total clockwise moment equals the total anticlockwise moment.

items.good: After the reveal, your notebook got the idea: “it is through the pivot”.
items.fix: You predicted the nut would turn more. If the force points through the pivot, the perpendicular distance is zero, so the moment is zero and nothing turns. The word is perpendicular distance, not height.
items.model: The force acts through the pivot, so the perpendicular distance is zero, and moment = force × 0 = 0. The nut does not turn.

entries.subject: History
entries.title: The Black Death: what changed?
entries.summary: You finished both paragraphs, and your cultural one has a real So What in it: “They were so desperate that they resorted to … hurting themselves to show God that they were sorry … in the hope that God might … forgive them”. That points straight back at the whipping and says what they hoped for. You also put the flagellants in Germany this time, which is right. You marked yourself 0 on almost everything: you earned more than that, so tick what you actually did. Three things to fix.
entries.next: Read the two “aim for” paragraphs in your email. Then, on this page, write a new Evidence + So What on S4 (the 1351 law) by yourself: what does that law tell us the lords wanted or feared? Read it out loud to Dad.

items.good: “The lords who paid the peasants were forced to pay more if they wanted their workers to stay as many had dropped dead from the plague” is a clear cause and effect. Your Point box said the same thing well.
items.fix:
1. Your facts are not followed by a So What. After each fact, ask: what does this tell us the peasants or the lords wanted or feared? “Society slowly began to collapse” is too big a claim and does not point back at one fact.
2. Add a date or a law. S4 is the best fact for this paragraph: the lords passed a law to stop wages rising. Ask yourself why they wanted that.
items.model: After 1349, surviving peasants demanded higher wages, and some left their manor to work for whoever paid most. This suggests that peasants now knew their work was valuable and wanted a better life than the one their lord had given them.

items.fix: 3. Claim check: Serfdom is not a village. It was the system where unfree peasants (villeins) had to work their lord’s land for free and were not allowed to leave. So “villages (like Serfdom) died out” needs rewriting. Also, villages were deserted for several reasons, not because peasants got richer and moved out.
items.model: Over the next 100 years serfdom slowly died out in England, as more peasants paid their rent in money and were free to move.

items.good: Your flagellant So What is grounded: it points back at the whipping and says what they hoped (that God would forgive them). “In Germany” is a correct, specific place.
items.fix: Your first fact (praying, processions, pilgrimages) has no So What after it. What does begging God to take the plague away show they believed caused it? Also: “torture” means someone else hurting you, so “hurting themselves” is the better word. Capital letters for England, Germany and the Black Death.
items.model: In 1348–49 people prayed, led processions and went on pilgrimages to beg God to end the plague. This suggests they believed the plague was God’s punishment for sin, so the only cure was to show God they were sorry.

entries.subject: Science
entries.title: Days 1–2: Pressure
entries.mark: Calculations 3 / 6 first time (6 / 6 in the end) · Written 3 / 9
entries.summary: Your multiple-choice was strong: snowshoes, heated gas, mountain air all right. And look at your calculations: you got the first ones wrong, then the last two (c5, c6) right first time, including the hard “find the area” one. That's learning in one sitting. Your written answers start well, then stop one link too early, so they lose the last mark. You gave yourself 5 / 9 for writing; I'd give 3 / 9.
entries.next: Before the test: write P = F ÷ A at the top of every calculation, then cover the letter you want. And for every “Explain” question, finish with the word pressure: “…so the pressure is smaller / bigger.”

items.good: c2, c5 and c6 right first time, and you fixed every wrong one.
items.fix: Three of the four wrong first tries used the wrong sum: multiplying when you should divide, or the other way round. Pressure = force ÷ area. Force = pressure × area. Area = force ÷ pressure.

items.q: Which unit is the same as 1 N/m²?
items.fix: A newton is a force, not a pressure.
items.model: 1 N/m² = 1 pascal (Pa).

items.q: Bike pump with your finger over the end
items.fix: No air escapes, so there isn't less air. The same air is squeezed into a smaller space.
items.model: The particles are closer together, so they hit the walls more often, so the pressure goes up.

items.good: “The wide tyres have a bigger surface area” is right.
items.fix: You spread the pressure, but it's the weight (force) that's spread. And “the force is larger” is wrong: the weight stays the same. You never said the pressure gets smaller.
items.model: The wide tyres have a bigger area touching the ground, so the tractor's weight is spread over a bigger area. This means the pressure on the ground is smaller, so it sinks less.

items.good: You knew the bag puffs up because of a pressure difference.
items.fix: Nothing changes inside the bag: the air inside is the same. What changes is outside. Start with the mountain.
items.model: Higher up, there is less air above, so the atmospheric pressure outside the bag is lower. The air inside is now at a higher pressure than the air outside, so it pushes the bag outwards and it puffs up.

items.good: “The air in the tyre gets hotter” and “the particles … faster”: a good start to the chain.
items.fix: Say what the faster particles do to the walls.
items.model: The air in the tyre gets hotter, so its particles move faster. They hit the walls of the tyre harder and more often, so the pressure increases.

entries.subject: Science
entries.title: Day 3: The digestive system
entries.summary: Brilliant recall: every multiple-choice question right, and your bread journey was a full-marks answer, in order, with every organ named. Your self-marking was honest too. The one to fix is the adaptations question: you named the adaptations but didn't say how each one helps.
entries.next: Learn the three adaptations as three Because Chains: villi → big surface area → more absorbed at once; thin wall → short distance → into the blood fast; capillaries → carry food away.

items.good: You picked the right two adaptations: villi and a thin wall.
items.fix: “Makes it easier to absorb” doesn't say why: the mark is for surface area. It's food molecules that move into the blood, not the blood that diffuses. And enzymes catalyse (speed up) digestion; the food itself is digested, not catalysed.
items.model: Villi give the small intestine a big surface area, so more food is absorbed at once. The wall is thin, so molecules only have a short distance to travel into the blood. Each villus has lots of capillaries, which carry the food away.

items.good: Every stage, in order: saliva, oesophagus, acid and juices, digestion and absorption, water absorbed, rectum and anus. Using “carbohydrases” and “glucose” was a bonus.
items.fix: Tiny polish: say the glucose is absorbed into the blood.
items.model: The villi absorb the glucose into the blood.

entries.subject: Science
entries.title: Day 4: Contact forces
entries.summary: Every short question right, including both Hooke's Law calculations first time. Your “500 N forwards” was right too: the page marked it wrong because of the words after the number, which I've fixed. The written questions are where the marks went: one answer was one link long, and you skipped the spring one.
entries.next: Go back to e2 (spring and rubber band) and have a go: it's the graph you saw in s4, plus one more line. Then redo e1 using the model.

items.good: “500 N forwards” is exactly right: size and direction.
“Less friction” is the key idea.
items.fix: One link isn't an explanation. Say why there's less friction, and what that does to the car.
items.model: New tyres have deep tread, so they grip the road. Worn tyres are smooth, so there is less friction between the tyres and the road. This means the car slides more easily and takes longer to stop, so it is more likely to skid.

items.good: Being honest that you weren't sure is better than guessing.
items.fix: You already know half of this: in s4 you said a straight line through the origin means the spring obeys Hooke's Law. A rubber band stretches more and more easily, so its graph curves.
items.model: The spring's graph is a straight line through the origin, so it obeys Hooke's Law: the extension is proportional to the force. The rubber band's graph is curved, so it does not obey Hooke's Law.

entries.subject: Science
entries.title: Day 5: Breathing
entries.summary: The bell-jar questions were all right, and your lung-volume method was full marks. Two short questions went wrong in the same place: which way the pressure goes when you breathe in, and which way the diaphragm moves when you breathe out. Then in the mock warm-up half an hour later you got the breathing-out question right. That's the fix working.
entries.next: Tuesday, after Fix your mistakes: do Science Week 5, “One rule, three places” (15 minutes). It's the same rule in breathing, the bike pump and the crisp bag.

items.fix: More space means lower pressure, not higher. The chest gets bigger, so the air inside is more spread out.
items.model: When you breathe in, the chest volume increases, so the pressure inside decreases. It is now lower than the air pressure outside, so air is pushed in.

items.good: You knew it relaxes.
items.fix: When it relaxes it moves back up into a dome. Down is for breathing in.
items.model: When you breathe out, the diaphragm relaxes and moves up.

items.q: Volume and pressure in the chest
items.good: Your breathing-out sentence was right: “the pressure increases cos the volume decreases”. And “the muscles in your ribs contract” is the right start.
items.fix: Two things. Breathing in, the volume increases (you wrote decreases). And you never mentioned the diaphragm, so that tick wasn't earned, while your breathing-out pressure point deserved one. Finish each half with the air: in or out.
items.model: When you breathe in, the rib muscles contract and the ribs move up and out, and the diaphragm contracts and moves down. So the volume of the chest increases and the pressure decreases, and air is pushed into the lungs. When you breathe out, the muscles relax, the ribs move down and in and the diaphragm moves up, so the volume decreases, the pressure increases and air is pushed out.

items.good: A clear method in the right order: lines on the bottle, upside down in water, breathe out through a tube, read the volume. Full marks, and you marked it accurately.

entries.subject: Science
entries.title: Week 4: moments and the lever chain
entries.mark: Short questions 7 / 8 · Door question 1 / 2 (you gave yourself 2)
entries.summary: Clockwise and anticlockwise are fixed: both right this time, which was a mistake last week. The see-saw calculation was right first time. Two things are still loose: why pulling along a spanner does nothing, and finishing the chain with the force.
entries.next: The Science Week 5 warm-up has both of these. Two minutes.

items.fix: Pulling works fine on a spanner if you pull sideways. The problem is the direction: along the spanner, the force goes straight through the nut.
items.model: The line of the force goes through the pivot, so the perpendicular distance is zero and the moment is zero.

items.q: Pushing the door at the handle
items.good: “The moment is the force multiplied by the distance” is the right start, and you used the hinge as the pivot.
items.fix: The question asks why it's easier. Easier means less force. End with the force, not the moment. This is the same fix as last week, so watch for it.
items.model: The handle is further from the hinge, so the distance is greater. Moment = force × distance, so a smaller force is needed to make the same moment, which makes it easier to open.

entries.subject: Maths
entries.title: Week 4: dividing fractions
entries.mark: Calculations 6 / 7 · Meaning questions 0 / 2 · Explain 0 / 2 (you gave yourself 1)
entries.summary: Your method is solid: every keep, flip, change calculation right first time, including the mixed numbers and the juice question. What's missing is the meaning: what dividing by a fraction actually asks. That's why 4 ÷ [[1/3]] and “bigger or smaller?” went wrong.
entries.next: Maths Week 5 warm-up: three “how many fit?” questions. Say “how many quarters fit into 3?” in your head before you answer.

items.fix: Ask “how many thirds fit into 4?” Each whole has 3 thirds.
items.model: 4 ÷ [[1/3]] = 12, because there are 3 thirds in each whole, and 4 × 3 = 12.

items.fix: Dividing by something less than 1 gives a bigger answer: more than one piece fits into each whole.
items.model: Bigger, because [[2/3]] is less than 1, so more than five lots of [[2/3]] fit into 5.

items.good: You described the method correctly: flip [[1/2]] to 2 and multiply.
items.fix: That's the rule, not the reason. The mark scheme wants “how many halves fit into 6”, so neither tick was earned.
items.model: Dividing by a half asks how many halves fit into 6. Each whole has 2 halves, so 6 wholes have 6 × 2 = 12 halves.

entries.subject: History
entries.title: Week 4: the Black Death, So What?
entries.summary: You spotted every problem in your old sentences: the drifting So What, the hindsight, the missing place and date. Your herbs rewrite is a real So What about a belief. The cleaning-the-streets rewrite was left as “C”, so that one is still to do.
entries.next: History Week 5 takes the same skill to money and work: what did peasants want, what did lords fear?

items.q: Rewrite So What 2 (bad air and herbs)
items.good: “Bad air was normally cured by sweet smells so they used herbs to block out the miasma”: it points back at the herbs and says what people believed. You under-marked it.
items.fix: Make the belief the main clause so the examiner can't miss it.
items.model: This suggests people believed disease travelled in bad-smelling air, so they carried sweet herbs to block the miasma.

items.fix: Not attempted. Use the reference: in 1349 the king ordered London's streets to be cleaned because of the smell. Then a So What about what they believed.
items.model: In 1349 King Edward III ordered the streets of London to be cleaned because of the foul smell. This suggests people believed the stink itself carried the disease, so removing filth would protect them.

entries.subject: English
entries.title: Week 4: the empty town
entries.summary: Every analysis question right: you can tell an effect from a retelling, and you picked the strongest So What every time. The last task needed your Tsunami Girl book, which you didn't have.
entries.next: English Week 5 gives you the passage on the page (a real GCSE extract from A Christmas Carol), so the last task is all yours: write the paragraph.

items.good: Saying you couldn't find one is honest.
items.fix: When the book isn't with you, pick any short phrase you remember about the zone and analyse that.
